You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

The test method `testLocaleIndependence()` in the `org.apache.commons.codec.language.RefinedSoundexTest` class encodes strings using different locales and then compares the encoded results. The test sets different locales and encodes the same data with the encoder for each locale. If the locale is not the default locale, the encoded result is compared with the encoded result for the default locale.

The bug report mentions fixing case-insensitive string handling in the language codecs and refers to a common bug. The test method seems to be related to locale independence rather than case-insensitive string handling. 

To locate the fault, we need to investigate the encoding logic of the `StringEncoder` implementation being tested in the `makeEncoder()` method. Additionally, we should check the implementation of the `encode()` method in the `StringEncoder` class to see if there are any issues related to case-insensitive string handling.

Let's first inspect the `makeEncoder()` method to see how the `StringEncoder` instance is created.

The `makeEncoder()` method in the `RefinedSoundexTest` class creates a new instance of `RefinedSoundex` as the `StringEncoder` implementation.

The `encode(String pString)` method in the `RefinedSoundex` class simply delegates to the `soundex(String)` method, which is likely to perform the actual string encoding based on the Refined Soundex algorithm.

Given the simplicity of the encoding logic, the fault related to case-insensitive string handling is unlikely to be in the encoding method itself. However, the fault may lie in the comparison logic in the test method `testLocaleIndependence()`. 

The test iterates over different locales and compares the encoded strings. If case-insensitive string handling is an issue, the comparison logic may be incorrectly assuming case sensitivity or not handling case-insensitive comparisons appropriately.

To fix the case-insensitive string handling, you should review the comparison logic in the `testLocaleIndependence()` method of the `RefinedSoundexTest` class. Ensure that the comparisons are case-insensitive if needed or update the logic to account for case insensitivity when comparing the encoded strings.

The fault may lie in the comparison logic of the test method `testLocaleIndependence()`.

Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
